title: Minimum Size Subarray in Infinite Array
statement:
Picture an endless array `infinite_nums` built by writing out `nums` again and again: a copy of `nums`, then another copy, and so on forever.

Return the length of the shortest contiguous subarray of `infinite_nums` whose elements add up to exactly `target`. If no subarray has that sum, return `-1`.
notes:
## Intuition

All values are positive, so a long subarray is just whole copies of `nums` plus a leftover piece: any stretch of `n` consecutive elements in `infinite_nums` sums to `total`, the sum of `nums`. So the answer uses `cycles = floor(target / total)` full copies (`cycles * n` elements) and then needs a short piece summing to `rest = target % total`. That piece is shorter than `n`, but it may wrap from the end of `nums` to its start, so search it in `nums` written twice. With only positive numbers, a variable-size sliding window finds every window with a given sum.

The brute force starts at every index and extends until the sum reaches `target`; that can take up to `target` steps per start.

## Approach

1. Compute `total`, `cycles` and `rest`. If `rest` is 0, the whole copies alone are the answer: `cycles * n`.
2. Slide a window over indices `0` to `2n - 1`, reading `nums[index % n]`.
3. Add `nums[right % n]` to `windowSum`; while it exceeds `rest`, drop elements from `left`.
4. When `windowSum === rest`, keep the shortest length in `best`.
5. If no window matched, return `-1`; otherwise `cycles * n + best`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 2, 3]`, `target = 5`, so `total = 6`, `cycles = 0`, `rest = 5`. Window `[1, 2, 3]` has sum 6, so `left` drops the 1, leaving `[2, 3]` with sum 5: `best = 2`. Later windows such as `[3, 1]` or `[2, 3]` (wrapped) never do better, so the answer is `0 * 3 + 2 = 2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each of the `2n` positions enters and leaves the window at most once.
- Space: O(1): the doubled array is only simulated with `% n`.

## Pitfalls

- Do not slide over `infinite_nums` up to `target` itself; `target` can be 10^9 while `nums` has one element.
- The leftover piece can wrap around the end of `nums`; scanning `nums` only once misses those windows.
- When `rest` is 0 return `cycles * n` directly; the window search would look for an empty sum.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `total` | sum of one copy of `nums` |
| `cycles` | number of whole copies inside the answer |
| `rest` | the part of `target` left after the whole copies |
| `left`, `right` | window bounds over the doubled array |
| `windowSum` | sum of the current window |
| `best` | shortest window found with sum `rest` |

narration.3: Add up one copy of nums; every n consecutive elements of the infinite array sum to this.
narration.4: Whole copies of nums that fit inside target.
narration.5: What remains to be covered by a piece shorter than one copy.
narration.6: If nothing remains, the whole copies alone hit target exactly.
narration.7: Their length is cycles copies of n elements.
narration.13: Slide over nums written twice, so the piece may wrap around the end.
narration.14: Grow the window by the next element, using % n to read the doubled array.
narration.15: Values are positive, so a sum above rest can only shrink by dropping from the left.
narration.16: Remove the leftmost element from the window...
narration.19: This window sums to exactly the remainder.
narration.23: No window fits means no subarray works; otherwise add the whole copies to the best piece.
